t.1.17.1: The Sūta said: Then the Daityas and Dānavas, banded together, seized the finest armour and weapons of many kinds and rushed upon the Devas.
t.1.17.2: Then the mighty god Viṣṇu, the lord, accompanied by Nara, took that amṛta and carried it away from the lords of the Dānavas.
t.1.17.3: Then all the hosts of gods, having received the amṛta from Viṣṇu, drank it at that time, while a tumultuous commotion was underway.
t.1.17.4: Then, while the gods were at that time drinking the longed-for amṛta, the Dānava Rāhu, in the form of a god, drank it too.
t.1.17.5: Then, when the amṛta had reached the throat of that Dānava, it was made known by the Moon and the Sun, out of a desire for the welfare of the gods.
t.1.17.6: Then the Blessed One, who bears the discus as his weapon, forcefully cut off with his discus the adorned head of that one as he was drinking the amṛta.
t.1.17.7: That huge head of the Dānava, like the peak of a mountain, severed by the discus, fell, shaking the surface of the earth.
t.1.17.9: And the blessed Hari too, casting off his incomparable woman's form, made the Dānavas tremble with many kinds of fearsome weapons.
t.1.17.8: Then the mouth of Rāhu formed an eternal, unyielding enmity with the Moon and the Sun, and even today it swallows the two of them.
t.1.17.10: Then, near the salt ocean, there began a great battle between the gods and the asuras, more terrible than all others.
t.1.17.11: Very broad, sharp lances fell by the thousands, and javelins with very sharp points, and weapons of many kinds.
t.1.17.12: Then the Asuras, split open by the discus and shattered by swords, spears and maces, fell upon the surface of the earth, vomiting much blood.
t.1.17.14: Their limbs smeared with blood, the slain great Asuras lay there like mountain peaks reddened with minerals.
t.1.17.13: In that dreadful battle, heads severed by paṭṭiśa blades, still adorned with nets of refined gold, fell ceaselessly then.
t.1.17.16: As they struck one another in battle with yellow iron clubs, and with their fists when at close quarters, the din seemed to touch the very sky.
t.1.17.15: Cries of “alas, alas!” arose here and there by the thousands from those hacking at one another with weapons, while the sun turns blood-red.
t.1.17.17: "Cut! Pierce! Charge forward! Strike him down! Advance!" Such exceedingly dreadful cries were heard there on every side.
t.1.17.18: While that terrible, fear-inspiring battle was raging thus, the two gods Nara and Nārāyaṇa came together to the field of combat.
t.1.17.19: There, seeing the divine bow of Nara, the blessed Viṣṇu too called to mind his discus, the slayer of the Dānavas.
t.1.17.20: Then, the moment it was merely thought of, there came from the sky the discus Sudarśana, of great radiance, scorcher of enemies, equal to the fire, its circular rim unblunted, terrible, invincible and supreme.
t.1.17.22: Then that swift weapon, its splendor equal to the fire of Antaka, hurled by the hand of the best of men in battle, fell again and again, tearing apart the sons of Diti and Danu by the thousands.
t.1.17.21: That terrifying discus, come to him and radiant like a blazing fire, Acyuta, whose arms were like an elephant's trunk, hurled forth, swift and of towering speed, greatly radiant, the shatterer of enemy cities.
t.1.17.24: Then the Asuras, undaunted in spirit, mighty in strength and having the splendour of clouds that have poured out their rain, rose into the sky by the thousands and again and again harassed the host of gods with mountains.
t.1.17.23: Blazing here and there like fire and licking all around, it forcibly cut down those hosts of asuras; hurled again and again into the sky and onto the earth, it then drank blood in battle like a piśāca.
t.1.17.25: Then from the sky there fell, striking terror, great mountains together with their trees, looking like clouds of many kinds, their peaks and ridges crumbling away, crashing swiftly into one another with a thunderous roar.
t.1.17.26: Then the earth, together with its forests, shook, struck on every side by the falling of great mountains, as the warriors roared fiercely at one another again and again while the battle raged violently on the battlefield.
t.1.17.27: Then Nara, with great arrows whose tips were adorned with the finest gold, covered the pathway of the sky, splitting the mountain peaks with his feathered shafts, in that greatly terrifying battle with the hosts of Asuras.
t.1.17.28: Then the great Asuras, harried by the Suras, entered the earth and the salt-watered ocean, having beheld Sudarśana, blazing like a kindled fire, gone up into the sky and enraged.
t.1.17.29: Then, having won the victory, the gods sent Mandara, well honored, back to its own place; and the clouds, having made the sky and heaven resound on every side, then departed the way they had come.
t.1.17.30: Then the gods, having attained supreme and abundant joy, put the amṛta securely away; and Balabhid, together with the immortals, gave that treasure of amṛta to Kirīṭin to guard.
